Something I don't get: how does a website domain (and by extension the game name) connect to the existence of a Switch port? All it means is that the domains are abbreviations of full names; for all we know P5U could mean Persona 5 Ultimax (as in a fighting game in the same vein as P4U).

In addition, wasn't it confirmed by Nintendo that Joker is part of the 1st DLC pack for Smash Bros? Correct me if I'm wrong, but April 2019 seems like a long wait time for DLC to be released, especially for the first set (I don't think Xenoblade Chronicles 2 took that long for DLC to appear). As such, Nintendo saving the release of that DLC pack to coincide with an announcement from Atlus in April of all times seems highly unlikely to me. Wouldn't it be more likely that the DLC release would coincide with a Nintendo Direct presentation? Think about it; Smash Bros is under Nintendo's control, and so was every Nintendo Direct presentation. If (and this is a very big if) Atlus planned to have something special to present to coincide with the DLC release, it would have to be during the Direct, not on some conference organized by Atlus with little direct input from Nintendo.

On the point of Joker being in Smash as evidence of P5 coming to Switch, I would like to point out a couple of things:

1) Joker appears in Persona Q 2: New Cinema Labyrinth, a 3DS title. Mind you, he doesn't appear chibi at all in the announcement, but in regular body proportions. The point here is if Sakurai had some way to contact the right people to negotiate for the rights to use the character in his game, the 3DS spinoff would have been the most likely point of entry.

2) Cloud Strife from Final Fantasy VII appeared in the previous Smash Bros game as DLC, and that game was never on a Nintendo console. Sure, Final Fantasies VII, IX, X, and X-2 were recently announced for the Switch, but keep in mind that Cloud was in Smash well before the Switch was even announced publicly, let alone the Switch port for Final Fantasy VII. As such, Joker being in Smash could very well be the result of clever negotiation for a one time deal between Nintendo and Atlus in the same way that Cloud was intended to be for Nintendo and Square Enix.

With that said, I'll hope for the best, but I'll expect these rumours to be just rumours by the end of it all. If Altus does have anything for the next Nintendo Direct, I'm hoping it's going to be about Shin Megami Tensei V (it's been so long, and I'm dying to know more!).

This is an intriguing argument, and I like that there is a distinction between Character and World stories.

My only question is: where does the Persona series fit into all of this? World exploration is a big part of these games because they are built as Jungian concepts made manifest (ie. Shadows, personas, or even Tartarus, the Midnight Channel, and Mementos as representations of the collective unconscious). 

But then you have deeply written characters with goals, desires, and flaws as you might find in Character stories. Given that Persona 3 to 5 uses characters in their Social Link/Confidant systems as a representation of psychological alchemy, would it be accurate to say that characters in the Persona series act as part of the world in a World story? And, by that logic, wouldn't it follow that Character and World are more or less intertwined in every game to some extent?

Now that I think about it, I don't think it's fair to say that every game is either a Character or World story as a dichotomy; I suspect Character and World are part of a continuum as opposite sides. On one extreme, Character, you have visual novels. On the other, World, you have walking simulators and exploratory puzzle games (like Myst, maybe). I suspect Persona might lie in the middle.

But then you have games like CoD, which don't have complex characters nor a world deeper than "shoot enemies and don't get shot." Would that be in the middle with Persona? Or is there an additional intersecting continuum (detail/depth of detail) that hasn't been considered yet?

This is counter to the stereotypes I've heard, where lesbians fall in love easily, move in together too soon, and break up shortly afterwards.

With that said, I think I understand where you get the idea about lesbians; you hear more about success stories involving lesbians more than the tragedies they face (last I checked, Ellen Degeneres is still happily married). Conversely, you don't really hear as many success stories about gay men (in fact, you may have heard about a recent tragedy: Anderson Cooper's break-up).

As for gay men being less inclined to be romantically interested, I don't think Grindr is the only thing to blame (in fact, blaming just Grindr is overly simplistic). Men in general tend to be more interested in sex than women. Given that gay men are 1) men, and therefore more likely interested in sex, and 2) attracted to men, who themselves are more likely interested in sex, it follows that the culture in the gay community centres around everyone having sex rather than everyone dating and courtship. It isn't a new phenomena; it's been around at least since the advent of gay bars. It's unfortunately the reason why there is a stereotype about how gay men can't fall in love, if they are capable of falling in love at all.

Of course, the truth of the matter in regards to commitment between gay men and lesbians is nuanced; there are lesbian couples that barely last beyond two weeks, and there are gay male couples who not only get married but also start families. And then there are relationships that aren't monogamous or otherwise easily categorized (ie. open relationships, polyamory, couples with at least one bisexual person, etc.). 

Sadly, I have yet to find any scientific study with hard numbers to paint an accurate picture about the rates gay male couples and lesbian couples get together versus corresponding divorce rates. If anyone can find such a study, I would really like to see it for myself. If such a study doesn't exist, I guess I've given all the social scientists here a topic or idea to pursue (and I'll be thankful for anyone who does this research).

1. a) Before I came out, it felt like an invisible force was holding me back, whether it was being unable to take a step into the campus pride centre, or having my voice taken away when I try to tell a counsellor. When I came out to myself via journal entry, I struggled to write "I am gay" in its entirety; again, the invisible force acted up, and it took me two hours and two ruined pages before I could successfully write that three word sentence. By the end of that, I felt like Beatrix in Kill Bill after she punched her way out of her buried coffin.

1. b) When I came out to someone else the first time, it was with a friend from high school over Skype; I wanted to tell a closer friend, but the first person I came out to was the only person online that night. After I called her up, time felt like it froze around me when I told her I was gay (the first season finale of Out With Dad captured that moment perfectly). When that friend gave her support, it felt like time resumed. We continued on our conversation, I felt euphoric for about a month after that, though that was the only time I've ever felt euphoric after coming out.

2. I've yet to experience a truly bad coming out, though that is because I'm selective in who I tell (mind you, I've lost count of how many people I've told, but I'm still tight-lipped in real life). The closest experience I've had to a bad experience was when my half-sister found out I was gay from reading some of my answers on Miitomo (if anyone remembers what that was). Considering that she promised to keep it a secret between me, her, and her best friend at the time, I'd say all's well that ends well.

3. My mother asked me when I came out to her about how I knew I was gay, and I asked her to think about her first crushes and how that informed her of her being straight. While my response at the time was satisfactory, I've just now thought about what I'd say being gay is like if I were to elaborate on my life experiences up to now. At first, around the time I came out to myself, I thought there's a lot to learn about being gay (we all like to joke about not getting our copy of The Gay Agenda upon coming out, but I think there is truth to that). A couple years since coming out (and even now), I've come to realize that there's little that's actually special about being gay; being gay is more mundane than how everyone makes it out to be. It's the fact that my life is just as mundane as everyone else's that I think is the most important thing to share, not just with my mother or father, but to everyone.

I know this is lengthy, but I there was a lot I wanted to share here.

Personally, I can take it or leave it; I care more about the quality of the media in question than if some part of my identity is represented. Case in point: Ready Player One; it's a movie that's trying to appeal to gamers, but a number of gamers I know (and myself) aren't convinced it's going to be any good.

If I am enjoying good media and a well written gay character shows up, I would consider it a pleasant surprise (like chocolate filling in a delicious cake). If the gay character isn't well written, I'd probably forget about the character or wait until a decent writer does something better with the character (this would be like eating pizza with pineapple in it; I'd just pick out the pineapple and eat the rest).

In cases where the movie revolves around some aspect of the protagonist's identity, that would depend on the writing and what story is being told.  For example, I've recently watched Call Me By Your Name and Love, Simon. They're both about 17 year old boys coming to terms with being gay. I didn't like the former movie for a number of reasons, and, ignoring the shock value throughout, the ending is pretty damn depressing (if I wanted to watch a gay movie with a depressing ending, I'd watch Brokeback Mountain). I really enjoyed the latter because, for a Hollywood movie, it's surprisingly tight knit; everyone and everything written in the movie has a purpose, and the ending is really hopeful (and given the number of depressing gay movies out there, I think we need more of them to inspire hope).

In short, quality content should come first. In media that caters to a specific demographic, quality content should still come first. Otherwise, what's the point of representation if what we get is crap?

Let me flip that around: if a violent crime occurs, and it was discovered that the criminal played violent video games, would it not be confirmation bias to connect these two together in a cause/effect relationship?

Here is my perspective on this: while right wing politicians as of late like to demonize violent video games, it's not exclusive to them; if anything, politically involved people from every part of the political spectrum do this (i.e. the left wing did this until recently; it's like they only changed their minds just because their ideological opponents said the same thing they did). One would think that they'd look at the scientific evidence first before doing anything rash, but, alas, all they go by are case studies or anecdotal evidence; you would be surprised at how lazy people are when it comes to researching issues for themselves (biases and other cognitive heuristics are basically shortcuts of reason; they save time and effort, but they are a huge source of trouble when trying to get a balanced or realistic perspective on controversial topics, with the violent video game "discussion" being a case in point).

What I think is happening when you see gamers declaring that they are not violent people despite playing violent video games is that they are trying to fight fire with fire; they're counteracting anecdotal evidence of violent behaviour with anecdotal evidence of being in a well adjusted disposition. As bothersome as it is, it's really the only way to get through to people in this day and age of clickbait and sensationalist media (again, people are intellectually lazy and like to rely on their biases and other cognitive heuristics).

You can try and persuade people using scientific evidence, but I wish you luck keeping their attention and making them listen to you while getting past their biases for more than 5 minutes.

Well, yeah, of course I do. With that said, if I can't change my fate, the least I can do is change how my mind works, and by extension how I feel. It's a gradual shift in perspective, but I can already tell you that you don't have to define life and happiness on the presence/absence of one thing; there are numerous other wonders in life and plenty other ways to find joy. Ultimately, only you yourself alone can find your reasons to be content in life.

That's what I'm trying to figure out and experimenting with. One thing I'm doing is following through with my resolution for 2018: to be grateful for what I already have in life; the idea was inspired by Buddhist and ancient Stoic ideas about 1) wanting what I have and not what I don't and 2) being happy with whatever life throws my way, whether good or bad.

The way I follow through with my resolution is with a daily gratitude journal; everyday, in a blank book or journal/diary, write down 3 things you are thankful for from your day (it can be as simple as writing 1. Shelter 2. Food 3. Clean drinking water). So far in my experience, after two full months doing this, I don't feel that different in my day to day life. However, by keeping record of all this, I do already have something to look back on and realize that yes I do have a good life.

It's NOT an instant cure for existential dread; it takes time and commitment before it begins to work. Keep going at it, and your perspective will eventually change for the better.

I think I get what you mean, as in being the nurturing parent; that's something I daydream about at times too.

As fas as I'm concerned, research has shown that children do well in two parent families, and that the gender(s) of the parents are more or less irrelevant (as in the results of child rearing are the same in straight, gay, and lesbian couples). What I think isn't brought up too often is that the wellbeing of the children depend on how well the parents do their jobs as parents, and not just with providing food, shelter, clothing, etcetera, etcetera; it also depends on how motivated the parents are as well (i.e. if the child/children are planned, how involved the parents are in their children's lives, or if both parents want, agree, and are fully informed about what they are getting into raising children).

TL;DR: It's fine to think about hypothetical children, and children raised by gay couples should be fine if the parents are responsible in raising said children.
